name: Athenian democracy
summary: Athenian democracy was the system by which the adult male citizens of Athens governed themselves in the fifth and fourth centuries BCE: they voted directly in the Assembly, filled the Council, juries and most magistracies by lot, paid citizens for public service, and held officials to account by audits and removal. Its own statements stress equality before the law, open debate, advancement by ability and every citizen's duty to take part. It excluded women, slaves and resident foreigners, restricted citizenship to those of citizen descent, and ruled an empire of subject allies.
scope: The constitution of classical Athens after Cleisthenes and Ephialtes, in its mature form from about 460 to 322 BCE (including the restoration of 403), as described by the Athenian Constitution and the speeches Thucydides reports, by Demosthenes and in funeral orations; Cartwright and the Stanford Encyclopedia define it as direct democracy for laws with sortition for officials. It is a form of government, so most statements on economics, society and technology are null. It excludes modern representative democracy (its own entry) and the critics of Athens such as Plato and Aristotle.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: The city's greatness rested on its fleet and citizen army, and Pericles urges war rather than loss of independence.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Pericles says class considerations may not interfere with merit and poverty bars no one, and Cleisthenes' reforms made the constitution more democratic.

arbitrator-settles-disputes.rationale: Thucydides reports that Athens offered arbitration under the treaty and that Sparta later judged it had itself broken the arbitration clause.

bound-labor.rationale: Solon freed the people by forbidding loans on the debtor's person, which Ath. Pol. 9 names as the first of the most democratic features of his constitution.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: The Assembly voted to raise and spend funds and received the Council's reports on the accounts (Cartwright; Ath. Pol. 43, 47-48).

citizens-assembly.rationale: A Council of 500 and jury panels of thousands chosen by lot prepared the Assembly's agenda and judged major political cases (Ath. Pol. 43, 45; Cartwright).

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Ath. Pol. 42 says the franchise is open to all who are of citizen birth by both parents, enrolled in their fathers' demes.

clerical-rule.rationale: Religious affairs were run by magistrates chosen by lot or vote under the Assembly, not by a clergy holding the highest authority (Ath. Pol. 54, 57).

collective-defense.rationale: The Assembly accepted a defensive alliance with Corcyra in which each party had a right to the other's help against invasion, and refused an offensive one.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Ath. Pol. 24 says tribute, taxes and contributions of the allies supported more than twenty thousand Athenians.

conscription.rationale: Young citizens served two years as ephebes under public training and garrison duty, and the city dispatched its citizens on service (Ath. Pol. 42; Thuc. 2.39).

consent-of-governed.rationale: Citizens ruled themselves by their own votes, but Athens ruled its allies without their consent, and Cleon calls the empire a despotism.

constitutional-jury-trial.rationale: Ath. Pol. 45 records a law that no citizen may be put to death except by a court of law, and 41 says the courts hold supreme power.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Courts of lot-chosen citizens could strike down Assembly proposals as illegal (Ath. Pol. 45, 59), yet those courts were the people themselves.

death-penalty.rationale: Thieves who pleaded guilty were executed by the Eleven, others after a court conviction, and juries imposed the penalty of death (Ath. Pol. 45, 52).

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: Athens paid infirm paupers two obols a day and maintained war orphans at public expense (Ath. Pol. 49, 24; Thuc. 2.46).

democracy-best.rationale: Pericles presents the democratic constitution as a pattern for others, and the people restored it after the oligarchies of 411 and 404-403 despite costly decisions of the Assembly.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: Pericles calls the constitution a democracy because its administration favours the many, a test of who benefits and not only of how rulers are chosen.

democracy-needs-political-clash.rationale: Pericles says Athens treats discussion as an indispensable preliminary to wise action and not as a stumbling block.

direct-votes.rationale: The Assembly voted directly on laws, decrees, war, treaties and spending, and Ath. Pol. 41 says the people made themselves master of everything by their votes in the Assembly and the courts.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Pericles tells widows that the greatest glory is to be least talked of among men, and public life was reserved to male citizens (Cartwright).

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Ath. Pol. 41 shows the people taking supreme power by their own exertions, and Pericles ties authority to the many, not to a god.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Pericles says private well-being depends on the greatness of the state and that civic merit outweighs private demerits.

elective-rulers.rationale: Generals and military officers were elected in the Assembly and no office was hereditary, but most magistrates were chosen by lot (Ath. Pol. 43, 61).

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Athens maintained its league and made alliances such as that with Corcyra, and its fathers handed down the empire as a possession.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Pericles promises equal justice in private disputes, but women, slaves and resident foreigners were excluded from political rights (Cartwright).

experts-over-public.rationale: Pericles says ordinary citizens busy with their trades are still fair judges of public matters, and Athenagoras says none can hear and decide so well as the many.

filial-duty.rationale: A suit for injury to parents lay before the archon, and archon candidates were asked whether they treat their parents well (Ath. Pol. 55, 56).

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: The Athenian Assembly sent force against allies that revolted, such as Mytilene, to keep the empire together.

foreign-residents-local-vote.rationale: Resident foreigners (metics) were excluded from the Assembly and every other political body (Cartwright).

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: Women held no seat in any Athenian public body, which excluded any requirement of equal representation.

head-commands-forces.rationale: The Assembly elected the generals, assigned their duties and decided war and peace, with no head of state over it (Ath. Pol. 44, 61).

indirect-election.rationale: Generals and other officers were elected or allotted from the whole citizen body, not by delegates of lower councils (Ath. Pol. 44, 61).

land-redistribution.rationale: Ath. Pol. 40 contrasts Athens, which refused a general redistribution of land after the civil war, with other democratic parties that made one.

military-superiority.rationale: Pericles boasts of Athenian naval supremacy, of power greater than any hitherto known, and tells the people not to give up their empire.

minority-veto.rationale: Assembly decisions went by majority show of hands and were final, and the minority was bound (Cartwright; Ath. Pol. 44).

mixed-constitution.rationale: Athenagoras argues that the demos includes the whole state and oligarchy only a part, and that the many judge best, so power should not be shared with the few.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Athens treated hereditary one-man rule as tyranny and honoured those who ended it, though the Ath. Pol. calls the early Pisistratid rule mild.

national-self-determination.rationale: Athens claimed leadership of the Greeks against Persia but ruled allies as subjects and suppressed their revolts, as at Mytilene (Thuc. 3).

native-born-offices.rationale: Only citizens of citizen birth could hold office, and archon candidates were examined on their parents and ancestry (Ath. Pol. 42, 55).

natural-rulers.rationale: Most offices went by lot to any citizen, presuming equal fitness, though generals were elected and Pericles says advancement went to capacity (Ath. Pol. 43, 62; Thuc. 2.37).

night-watchman-state.rationale: The state ran festivals, public pay, grain and market regulation, poor relief and public works, beyond defence, justice and property.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Pericles names obedience to the magistrates and the laws, written or unwritten, as the chief safeguard of Athenian life.

office-by-exam.rationale: Posts were filled by lot or by open vote, with a scrutiny (dokimasia) of birth and conduct rather than a test of learning (Ath. Pol. 43, 55, 61).

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Ath. Pol. 43 and 62 record that the Council, the juries and nearly all ordinary magistracies were filled by lot, while only military and a few financial posts were elected.

one-party-rule.rationale: Any citizen could speak and propose in the Assembly and the demos itself held power, which leaves no place for one party guiding the state.

parliament-supreme.rationale: The Assembly, with the courts, was the sovereign lawmaking body and no monarch stood above it (Ath. Pol. 41; Cartwright).

participatory-democracy.rationale: Pericles says Athens counts a citizen who takes no part in public duties as useless, and every citizen could speak and vote in the Assembly.

people-in-arms.rationale: Citizens served as hoplites and rowers, and Demosthenes urges Athenians to serve in person and not leave war to mercenaries, though paid mercenaries were used.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Cleisthenes' reforms grounded citizenship in the demes and the whole people, and Athenian authority rested on citizens' equal votes, not on personal oaths to lords.

political-decisions-consensus.rationale: The Assembly decided by majority vote, and the majority won the day (Cartwright), not by consensus.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Corn commissioners checked that corn sold at reasonable prices and that bread and barley meal were priced and weighed in proportion to grain (Ath. Pol. 51).

private-courts-defense.rationale: Courts were public bodies of lot-chosen citizens, and defence rested on the citizen army and fleet (Ath. Pol. 63-69).

promote-democracy-abroad.rationale: Athens set up democracies in allied states such as Samos, though it left Chios, Lesbos and Samos their own constitutions for a time (Thuc. 1.115; Ath. Pol. 24).

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Pericles stresses obedience to the written and unwritten laws, and Ath. Pol. 45 says the Assembly could only vote on matters first prepared and that illegal proposals were indictable, though decrees for single cases were common.

property-franchise.rationale: Pericles says poverty does not bar a man from public service, and the state paid for Assembly, jury and Council service (Ath. Pol. 41, 62).

public-access-to-information.rationale: Accounts, lists of confiscated property and magistrates' payments were read out or posted so that anyone could object (Ath. Pol. 43, 48).

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Indictments for impiety came before the King archon, and the Athenian people sentenced Socrates to death in 399 (Ath. Pol. 57; Cartwright).

recall-officials.rationale: In every prytany the people voted whether magistrates and generals should stay in office, and a rejected officer was tried (Ath. Pol. 43, 61).

replace-appointed-officials.rationale: Allotted magistrates held office for one year and none could hold the same office twice, apart from the Council, which allowed two terms (Ath. Pol. 62).

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Public service paid a few obols a day, and Cartwright says the money only covered expenses and attempts to profit from office were severely punished.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Impeachment before the Assembly, audits of every magistrate and suits against any official who disobeyed the laws gave citizens means to remove officers who broke the laws (Ath. Pol. 43, 45, 48, 59).

right-to-secede.rationale: Athens denied its allies the right to leave the league and put down revolts; Cleon calls the empire a despotism held by strength.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Sovereignty lay with the demos acting through the Assembly and courts, so a ruler regarded as sacred and of divine descent has no place (Ath. Pol. 41).

separate-church-state.rationale: The state ran the festivals and sacrifices through lot-chosen commissioners and heard indictments for impiety before the King archon (Ath. Pol. 54, 57).

separated-powers.rationale: The Assembly and courts held supreme power over everything (Ath. Pol. 41), yet the courts, the Council and the audits checked magistrates and Assembly proposals.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Pericles says Athenians obey the magistrates and the laws, and an Assembly proposal contrary to law exposed its mover to indictment for illegal proposal (Ath. Pol. 45, 59).

state-harmful.rationale: The Athenians held the polis to be the community that gives its citizens their greatness and their duties; Pericles says a man is ruined with a ruined country.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Athens led the Delian bloc and fought the Peloponnesian bloc for decades, joining Corcyra's alliance rather than staying out.

strong-leader.rationale: The law of ostracism was passed as a precaution against a popular leader making himself tyrant, and Athenians exiled men for being too powerful.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Free speech in the Assembly was prized, yet persistent critics risked charges of conspiring for tyranny and ostracism (Cartwright).

targeted-social-spending.rationale: The pension went only to those with less than three minas who were too crippled to work, after examination by the Council (Ath. Pol. 49).

term-limits.rationale: Allotted offices barred repeat tenure, but the elected military offices could be held any number of times (Ath. Pol. 62), so the record points both ways.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Pericles praises the empire the Athenians added to their inheritance and the power gained by forcing every sea and land open to their daring.

total-state.rationale: Pericles contrasts Athens with Sparta's state discipline: Athenians live as they please and do not watch one another.

vote-at-sixteen.rationale: Citizens were enrolled at eighteen, and enrolment tests sent those under age back to the boys (Ath. Pol. 42).

women-suffrage.rationale: Cartwright records that women, slaves and resident foreigners were excluded from the political process, and Athenian law gave only male citizens the vote.

missingStatements.text: Public officials should have their conduct audited when they leave office.
missingStatements.rationale: Every Athenian magistrate rendered accounts to lot-chosen auditors and could be prosecuted before a jury afterwards, as Ath. Pol. 48, 54 and 55 set out.

quotes.text: to whom all persons who have held any office must give in their accounts
to audit the accounts of the magistrates for each prytany

missingStatements.declined: A procedural detail accepted almost everywhere today.

missingStatements.text: Citizens should be paid from public funds for the time public duties take them from their work.
missingStatements.rationale: Athens introduced and raised pay for Assembly attendance because the poor stayed away without it, and paid jurors and Councillors (Ath. Pol. 41, 62).

quotes.text: At first they refused to allow payment for attendance at the Assembly; but the result was that people did not attend.
the jurors at the law-courts receive three obols

missingStatements.declined: Accepted almost everywhere today, so not contested.

missingStatements.text: Citizens should be able to vote to exile a person who has become too powerful for a free state, without a trial.
missingStatements.rationale: Ostracism let the Assembly exile a man by popular vote against over-powerful individuals, a law Cleisthenes passed as a precaution against tyranny.

quotes.text: This had originally been passed as a precaution against men in high office
those individuals considered too powerful or dangerous to the city were exiled for 10 years by popular vote

missingStatements.declined: A historical institution that no one proposes today.

notes: Themes searched in the Athenian Constitution (parts 1-69), Thucydides (Pericles, Cleon, Diodotus, Athenagoras, Alcibiades), Demosthenes, Lysias II and the reference works: government, citizenship, law and courts, war and empire, alliances, religion, welfare and public pay, property and debt, gender and exclusion. The record is silent on economics beyond public finance, on technology, ecology and culture, which are null. The Athenian Constitution is a description by the Aristotelian school, used here as the record of institutions. Plato and Aristotle on democracy are critics and are not used.
